China is increasingly relying on Russian oil amid the Iran War.

China’s imports of Russian oil rose by ~200,000 barrels per day in August, to ~1.6 million barrels per day, their highest since March.

This marks the 3rd consecutive monthly increase, bringing the cumulative gain over that stretch to ~500,000 barrels per day.

This is now above the levels seen in the last 4 months of 2025.

By comparison, China imported ~2.0 million barrels per day from Russia in February.

This comes as Middle East oil supplies have become more constrained and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, prompting Chinese refiners to turn increasingly to Russian crude.

Russian crude is increasingly filling the Middle East supply gap.

BREAKING: Short interest in the median S&P 500 stock is up to 3.2% of market cap, the highest level since 2009.

This is now approaching the 2008 Financial Crisis peak of ~3.8%.

By comparison, during the 2022 bear market, this percentage was ~1.7%.

Furthermore, short interest among the most heavily shorted 10% of S&P 500 stocks is up to 8.0% of market cap, the highest in 8 years.

Even during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble burst, short interest never surged to these levels.

The short trade is starting to look overcrowded.

World Labs co-founder Justin Johnson on how five photos from your phone could teach a robot to work in a room it has never seen:

"I think there's a couple different tech trees that people are working on. One is this notion of fully in-context learning. Maybe I've got a robotics foundation model, then I can demonstrate to the robot once how a task should be performed, and that's enough for the robot to figure out that task."

"Another version is what we're calling real-to-sim-to-real. Maybe I've got my pre-trained robotics foundation model, but I want to adapt it to this particular environment."

"Like this studio... You could come in here and take just a couple casual videos with your phone or a couple images with your phone, use Atlas to reconstruct the space, and now stage all kinds of robotics interactions in this studio space in particular."

"Literally you could do it in five minutes. Take five photos, upload it to Atlas, have it generate a simulation, describe in natural language what kind of task you want the robot to do, have an agent go build that simulation for you, RL fine-tune your general purpose robotics foundation model, and now you've got a robot... that's perfectly adapted to this space."

@jcjohnss on @MTSlive

Could US payrolls post another decline on Friday?

The number of hires fell by -278,000 in July, to 5.05 million, the lowest since February.

At the same time, total separations, the number of workers leaving their jobs through quits, layoffs or other departures, dropped -265,000, to 5.07 million, the lowest since April.

As a result, the difference between hires and separations widened to -18,000 in July, from -5,000 in June, its biggest gap since February.

This gap provides a rough indication of the direction of payroll growth and was broadly consistent with the official -23,000 payroll print in July.

Hires have now fallen below separations for 3 consecutive months, pointing to continued weakness in net job creation.

Because the hires and separations data feed into the payrolls calculation, the persistently negative gap suggests the official August payrolls figure could still have room to fall, raising the possibility of another negative print on Friday.

The US job market continues to appear weak.

Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel on the first-ever positive Phase 3 results for an individualized mRNA cancer vaccine:

"After working 10 years on an individualized treatment against cancer using mRNA technology, the Phase 3 was positive. It's the first time that there is an agent in melanoma that is better than Keytruda alone."

"It's the first time there is a cancer vaccine working. The field has been doing that for 20-plus years, I think more than 1,000 clinical trials that have all failed."

"We met the primary endpoint of the study, which was recurrence-free survival... And then, to our own surprise, because this was the first interim analysis... we met the secondary endpoint, which was distant metastasis-free survival."

@JorgeCondeBio @moderna_tx

tweets.text:
For over a decade, the bond market paid governments to borrow. That just flipped.

The 10-year term premium, the extra yield investors demand to hold long government debt, has gone from deeply negative to firmly positive across the US, Germany, and Japan. Japan now sits at the top of the range.

A positive and rising term premium means long yields climb no matter what the Fed does. It is the market charging to fund endless deficits again, and it feeds straight into mortgages, long-duration tech, and the government's own interest bill.

The decade of free deficits is over. Higher long rates are structural now, and the Fed cannot cut them away.

Affordability never resets on its own. The only thing that thaws this market is a big drop in mortgage rates. That is the box the Fed is in. $ITB

thread_tweets.text:
If you’re going to use the CSCO analog, I’d start the clock at the Netscape IPO in Aug 1995. That was the “killer app” moment, same as ChatGPT.

Cisco ran for another 4½ years.

And if you insist on starting at the 2000 peak, remember what happened next: Cisco had a few months of backlog that customers could cancel without penalty. Then the over-levered telcos blew up, WorldCom and Global Crossing went bankrupt, orders disappeared and Cisco ate a huge inventory charge.

Today the hyperscalers have $2.3T+ of cloud RPO stretching years, not quarters, across a much broader customer base, with some of the strongest balance sheets in the world funding the buildout.

And Cisco ultimately sold boxes that commoditized. While NVIDIA has CUDA + accelerators + networking + systems integration, which seems to me a lot closer to the kind of lock-in Apple kept.

tweets.text:
Very proud of my old friend here.

Scott Singer was my roommate for three years at Harvard and he's been one of my closest friends for thirty plus. He is the most honest, earnest, hardworking, decent family man I know, and I mean that literally, not as a figure of speech. He was doing philanthropy and student government as a little kid because he genuinely liked the work, and he never stopped. He was also a Jeopardy champion, which tells you something about a guy who always did the reading, even if it was often at 3am.

After two decades as an attorney and small business owner, Scott became mayor of Boca Raton and won three terms, which nobody there had ever done. He cut Boca's tax rate seven straight times and left the city with the lowest property tax of any full-service city in Florida. He got the Brightline station built and the first new public school in Boca in decades. He beat a five-way Republican field last month, and FL-25 may well decide the House.

I do want to be fair to Jared Moskowitz. He's a genuine moderate on some things. He voted for Laken Riley, the only Florida Democrat who did, he's said publicly he's against abolishing ICE, and he's been good on Israel and on antisemitism, which I appreciate. The DSA tried to primary him precisely because he isn't a raging leftist, and I'm not going to pretend he is one.

But there is one set of votes where he goes with his party every single time:

>Voted against the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (Jan '25, passed 218-206). Also voted against the 2023 version.
>Voted against requiring parental consent before a school changes a kid's "gender", pronouns or name (May '26, passed 217-198).
>Voted against stopping the military health plan from paying for gender transition surgeries and hormones for service members and their families (defense bill, adopted 219-208).
>Voted against keeping biological males out of girls' sports at Pentagon-run schools (defense bill, adopted 221-203).

As AOC recently said, "woke 1.0 was crazy." Personally I really don't want to find out what 2.0 entails, because I have a strong feeling it won't be good for Jews or kids or women or basic standards. For parents with daughters, these issues are crucial: who is in her locker room, who competes against her, whether her school tells you when something changes. On those votes, Moskowitz has never once broken with his party. Eight Democrats did on the parental consent bill. Not him.

Which brings me to something I worry about every day: my elderly parents live in New York City, where felony assaults remain 48% above 2019 levels and have risen every year since. Watching what has happened here under one-party rule has taught me to pay a lot more attention to how politicians actually vote when their party wants them in line. I'm not blaming Moskowitz for New York. But I want to feel confident where a pol will stand before it matters, than find out the hard way.

Last thing, on my own beat: South Florida will probably never host big data centers, because land and power cost too much. But rural counties across the country are getting real blue collar jobs and a much bigger tax base out of them. I hope each community can decide that for itself, rather than having blanket moratoriums imposed from above on the places with the most to gain. We outsourced our industrial production to China last generation and left the heartland hollowed out, poorer and disillusioned. I'd rather not run that experiment twice. Scott is far more likely to leave that call with local communities, where it belongs.

Disclosures: I donated to Scott's campaign. I also manage an ETF that holds data center and AI infrastructure companies. Views my own, not my employer's.

The DSA tried to primary him precisely because he isn't a raging leftist, and I'm not going to pretend he is one.

But there is one set of votes where he goes with his party every single time:

>Voted against the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (Jan '25, passed 218-206). Also voted against the 2023 version.
>Voted against requiring parental consent before a school changes a kid's "gender", pronouns or name (May '26, passed 217-198).
>Voted against stopping the military health plan from paying for gender transition surgeries and hormones for service members and their families (defense bill, adopted 219-208).
>Voted against keeping biological males out of girls' sports at Pentagon-run schools (defense bill, adopted 221-203).

As AOC recently said, "woke 1.0 was crazy." Personally I really don't want to find out what 2.0 entails, because I have a strong feeling it won't be good for Jews or kids or women or basic standards. For parents with daughters, these issues are crucial: who is in her locker room, who competes against her, whether her school tells you when something changes. On those votes, Moskowitz has never once broken with his party. Eight Democrats did on the parental consent bill. Not him.

Which brings me to something I worry about every day: my elderly parents live in New York City, where felony assaults remain 48% above 2019 levels and have risen every year since. Watching what has happened here under one-party rule has taught me to pay a lot more attention to how politicians actually vote when their party wants them in line. I'm not blaming Moskowitz for New York. But I want to feel confident where a pol will stand before it matters, than find out the hard way.

Last thing, on my own beat: South Florida will probably never host big data centers, because land and power cost too much. But rural counties across the country are getting real blue collar jobs and a much bigger tax base out of them. I hope each community can decide that for itself, rather than having blanket moratoriums imposed from above on the places with the most to gain. We outsourced our industrial production to China last generation and left the heartland hollowed out, poorer and disillusioned. I'd rather not run that experiment twice. Scott is far more likely to leave that call with local communities, where it belongs.
